summary: Defines Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST), a simple certificate management protocol for PKI clients that need client certificates and the related CA certificates. It builds on CMC messages sent over a secure transport, and supports keys generated by the client or by the CA.

plainLanguage.summary: Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST) defines how a PKI client requests CA certificates and client certificates from an EST server. It carries certificate-management messages over HTTPS and uses authentication and local policy to control requests.

subtitle: EST enrolls PKI clients for certificates through authenticated HTTPS requests.

tldr.problem: PKI clients need CA certificates and client certificates, and need a defined way to request them from an enrollment service.
tldr.mechanism: EST carries Certificate Management over CMS messages over HTTPS. Standard URI paths retrieve CA certificates, enroll clients and renew or rekey certificates.
tldr.outcome: The EST server authenticates and authorizes clients, while local CA policy decides whether to issue certificates. RFC 7030 has been updated by RFC 8951, RFC 8996 and RFC 9908.

today: RFC 7030 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8951, RFC 8996 and RFC 9908. Read it together with those updates.

sections.title: The Purpose of EST
sections.content:
EST profiles certificate enrollment for clients using Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) messages over a secure transport. It targets PKI clients that need client certificates and associated Certification Authority certificates.

An EST server sits between a client and a CA and performs functions traditionally assigned to a Registration Authority. This RFC does not specify how the EST server communicates with the CA. It also supports client-generated keys and an optional request for server-generated keys.
sections.plainLanguage: EST gives a client a defined way to ask an enrollment server for certificates. The server handles the request and applies the CA's policy.

sections.title: Messages over HTTP and TLS
sections.content:
EST has three layers: certificate request and response messages, HTTP for message transfer and operation selection, and TLS for transport security. The specification requires HTTPS over TCP and TLS 1.1 or later.

Each operation uses a path under /.well-known/est. The required operations are /cacerts, /simpleenroll and /simplereenroll. Optional paths provide full CMC, server-side key generation and CSR attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: EST messages travel in HTTP over a TLS-protected connection. The request path tells the server which certificate operation the client wants.

sections.title: Authenticating and Authorizing Both Sides
sections.content:
The client must authenticate the EST server before accepting responses, except for the defined CA-certificate bootstrap and Full CMC cases. Certificate-based TLS client authentication is recommended, and the server must support it. HTTP Basic or Digest authentication can be used over TLS, or the peers can use a suitable certificate-less TLS method based on a zero-knowledge protocol resistant to dictionary attacks.

Authentication does not itself decide whether a request is authorized. The client checks that the server is authorized to serve it, and the EST server uses local CA policy to decide whether a client may enroll. The CA controls the final issuance decision.
sections.plainLanguage: The client checks the server's identity, and the server checks the client's identity and request. The CA's local policy determines whether to issue a certificate.

sections.title: Getting CA Certificates and Enrolling
sections.content:
The client retrieves CA certificates with an HTTPS GET to /cacerts. A successful response has HTTP 200 and contains a certs-only CMC response. The server includes the current root CA certificate and certificates needed to build a chain. If the client bootstraps without a trusted CA, a human must verify the CA certificate out of band.

For initial enrollment, the client posts a PKCS #10 request to /simpleenroll. The request signature proves possession of the private key. Re-enrollment uses /simplereenroll; an unchanged public key renews the certificate, while a changed key rekeys it. A successful response contains the issued certificate.

An HTTP 202 response means processing is not complete. The server includes Retry-After, and the client waits at least that long before repeating the same request.
sections.plainLanguage: The client can first obtain the CA certificates, then submit a signed certificate request. The server returns the issued certificate or tells the client when to retry.

sections.title: Full CMC and Requested CSR Attributes
sections.content:
The optional /fullcmc operation carries Full CMC requests for certificate-management functions beyond simple enrollment. The optional /csrattrs operation lets a client ask which attributes the CA wants in a later request.

The server can list OIDs or attributes such as a requested key type or signature scheme. The client must ignore attributes it does not recognize. The server returns HTTP 204 or 404 when no CSR-attributes response is available.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients can use Full CMC for additional certificate-management functions. They can also ask which extra attributes the CA wants in a certificate request.

sections.title: Optional Server-Generated Keys
sections.content:
A client may use /serverkeygen to ask the server to create the key pair and certificate. The server ignores the public key and signature in the request's CSR. The TLS cipher suite must provide confidentiality so the private key is not exposed during transfer.

The client can request additional CMS encryption for the returned private key. The success response is multipart/mixed and contains the private key and certificate. The RFC recommends that servers not enable this operation by default and that clients request it only when there is a compelling operational benefit.
sections.plainLanguage: EST can optionally have the server generate a private key and return it to the client. Because sending private keys is risky, the RFC recommends additional encryption and cautious use of this option.

sections.title: Proof of Possession and Security Risks
sections.content:
A signed enrollment request proves that the client can use the corresponding private key. The client can also include the TLS session's tls-unique value in the signed request to link key possession to the authenticated TLS session; if the value is included, the server must verify it.

Basic authentication exposes the password to the EST server, so one-time credentials are recommended for obtaining an initial certificate. Trusting an implicit trust-anchor database does not establish that a server is authorized as an RA for the PKI. Server-side key generation sends private key material to the client, which the RFC describes as inherently risky.
sections.plainLanguage: The signed request can prove that the client has the requested private key and can link that proof to its TLS session. Clients must also consider password exposure, trust-anchor choice and the risks of receiving a server-generated private key.
